column2: Act Six
Star and Flower
“Fireworks!” Nono stopped short, crying out in wonder.

Fireworks were shooting up from the foot of the mountain, slashing the sky like meteors in reverse. They were flower seeds, blooming wildly in the darkness: dandelions like purple suns, cascading blue-green spider plants, roses woven from red and gold, white dahlias... Lu Mingfei had never seen anyone set off fireworks so extravagantly, flinging hundreds into the sky in a single instant and turning the night into a basket of flowers.
Nor had Lu Mingfei ever seen a face so beautiful. In the light of the fireworks, a faint glow flowed over Nono’s profile, along with fine traces of tears.
“Why am I dancing with you?”
“Probably because you don’t have the nerve to ask any of those pretty girls.”

Lu Mingfei and Fingel held each other in their arms, dancing a tango beside the dance floor... Both executed the forceful snaps of the head beautifully, their eyes fierce as two weasels fighting over an egg.

Around them were boys in black formal wear and girls in white gowns. The boys’ hair was combed into elegant, classical styles, slick with olive-scented pomade; the girls had taken even greater pains with theirs, and various perfumes drifted from their sumptuous curls.

The boys’ gleaming black dress shoes and the girls’ white dancing heels stepped across solid-wood parquet polished to a mirror shine. Enormous crystal chandeliers were reflected in the floor, their light now and then obscured by skirts flaring in a turn.

The story of why they were dancing was a long one... Back to the moment when Nono hauled the petty thief Lu Mingfei and the innocent bystander Fingel straight to the entrance of Amber Hall, where Caesar stood in white, applauding their arrival. Cold light flowed through his ice-blue eyes. Behind him stood the heads of the Student Council’s six departments, in ranks as immaculate as an army of a hundred thousand armored veterans.
“Right on time.” Caesar glanced at the Patek Philippe on his wrist and smiled faintly.
“Caesar smiled at you!” Fingel made a great fuss over it.
A shiver went through Lu Mingfei, because for a moment he had seen tender affection in that smile...
“I had ballet class this afternoon.” Nono walked up.
Caesar gently took her by the shoulders and exchanged an air kiss with her, a gesture as insufferably affected as it was elegant. “You look beautiful in this. I haven’t seen you wear it before.”

“I bought it when I went to China with Professor Guderian on business.” Nono shrugged. “You can’t possibly have seen all my clothes. I’ve still got the black robe and mask I wore to go trick-or-treating as a little ghost on Halloween. Want to see those?”
“If you knock on my door dressed like that, I’ll certainly give you candy,” Caesar said elegantly, taking Nono’s hand and leading her inside like an emperor.

Throughout this exchange he did not give anyone else so much as a glance. Whenever his gaze passed over another person, it was like a blade cutting through air. By the time Lu Mingfei and Fingel finished whispering and looked up, they were alone at the entrance. This was deeply embarrassing for Ricardo M. Lu and Fingel, senior to eight entering classes, who had just worked up the courage to shake Caesar’s hand.
“Was that supposed to put us in our place?” Fingel wondered.
“As men of honor, shouldn’t our dignity come first?” Lu Mingfei turned around. “If he won’t show us respect, we won’t show him any! We’re leaving!”

“Don’t! Brother, this is exactly when you have to stand your ground!” Fingel twisted him back around, raised a thumb, and encouraged his dignified junior like an older brother, pushing at his shoulders. “Go in! You were invited. What are you afraid of?”
Lu Mingfei did not move an inch. He gripped Fingel’s thumb tightly. “I trust you, senior! I, Lu Mingfei, am an honorable hero too, every bit as fine as you, Fingel! We go in together!”
“Then in we go! I’m the longest-serving student in this college. My rank has fallen to an unprecedented F, and I still haven’t dropped out. You think I’m afraid of Caesar?”

The Student Council officer handling check-in watched Lu Mingfei and Fingel enter Amber Hall sideways, all four hands clasped, facing each other, eyes locked, like a passionately enamored couple dancing a ferocious tango.

The lavish buffet soon convinced the roommates that their courage had paid off. Fingel quickly calculated the population of Amber Hall, while Lu Mingfei counted the lobsters, and together they reached an important conclusion: this social occasion was primarily about eating. Their generous host had provided one Australian lobster per person. The huge, scarlet creatures lay on ice, their backs split to reveal translucent white flesh. Abandoning caution, Fingel and Lu Mingfei set to with knives and forks, with all the force of tigers descending a mountain.
They enjoyed themselves enormously, right up until a white-gloved Student Council officer rang a small brass bell and the boys in black and girls in white appeared.

At the bell’s clear, sharp chime, the Student Council officers in the hall stopped talking. The crystal chandeliers in the center of the room lit up. Down the two curved staircases from the second floor came imposing young men in black on one side, and girls in white gowns and white silk gloves on the other. Silence filled the hall. The ball was about to begin. Everyone without a part to play had tactfully withdrawn to the corners, leaving only two fellows standing right in the middle with plates in their hands, still brandishing cutlery over their scarlet lobsters.
The two suddenly became aware of the situation. They stopped eating, stopped chattering, and wiped their mouths.
“We’re actually dancing?” Lu Mingfei stared, swallowing his mouthful of lobster.
“The one with mustard all over his mouth... that’s the new S-rank?” A girl on the stairs sounded astonished.
“They say he’s from a poor family,” her partner said. “But he works very hard!”
“What do you mean, ‘works very hard’? Is that a required footnote for kids from poor families?” Lu Mingfei thought. “My parents are just unreliable, that’s all!”
“He looks so sleazy... The one next to him... even sleazier.” Another girl frowned. “Those cheap suits... The fabric is just awful.”
“I heard he’s the principal’s illegitimate son, raised away from home all these years. He’s got connections,” someone else said.
“The principal would have an illegitimate son like that? My opinion of him just went down...”
“Sir, please clear the floor. The ballroom dancing is about to begin,” a waiter reminded him politely.
The comments had already left Lu Mingfei hanging his head and ready to flee; these words were a royal pardon. But he failed to escape. Fingel caught him!

“It’s been ages since I danced!” Fingel clapped his hands and uttered words for which, a few seconds later, he would scour the earth in search of a cure for regret. “When I first enrolled, I was the Elvis of my year!”
The waiter stared blankly at him.
“What are you looking at? Do I look like a man who doesn’t know social etiquette? I’m waiting here to dance!” Fingel glared, straightened his bow tie, and snapped his fingers smartly.
Fingel inspected the ladies on the stairs from head to toe. Lu Mingfei understood: cornered, he had no choice but to pick a partner and dance his way out of the embarrassment.

But everyone in the hall was paired off. Not one girl was free, and every girl Fingel looked at gave an identical little “Oh” and turned away, apparently responding as naturally as if she had spotted a cowpat.
He and Lu Mingfei were the only two “surplus” men in the room.

A deep-red curtain drew back on one side of the second floor, revealing a small orchestra tuning up. Its conductor was actually the cook who had delivered food to Lu Mingfei and Fingel late that night. Evidently the man was talented in all sorts of ways. The cook-cum-conductor was about to raise his baton when he turned and saw the two men standing at the center of the dance floor, the focus of every eye. He hesitated. With no instruction to proceed, the orchestra could only repeat the same little introduction over and over.
“A tango! My specialty!” Resolute determination shone in Fingel’s eyes. “Come on, brother! Don’t disgrace yourself. Hold firm! You and I will carve a beautiful way out and show Caesar!”
“Fantastic. Point me toward this way out!” Lu Mingfei answered his senior’s courage.

“I’m glad to see that spirit. Now, my dear junior, you take the lady’s steps...” Fingel slipped an arm around Lu Mingfei’s waist, took his hand, and snapped his fingers dashingly at the conductor upstairs. “Let’s rock!”

It was the first time Lu Mingfei had seen Fingel radiate such powerful presence, such a fearless, roving-hero spirit. A girl with a special weakness for young gangsters might have felt her heart stir for this scruffy man. But Lu Mingfei was no woman, and events would prove that every future occasion on which Fingel’s heroic spirit soared would lead them into a desperate situation... as utterly... desperate... as a situation could be.
The music began; skirts spun. Under overwhelming external pressure, the two weasels could only cling to each other.

A faint haze of perfume filled the air. Evidently the guests had all taken the same dance class and learned from the same teacher. Their movements were elegant, their positions precise. They formed a rectangular array, then spread into a circle, the men in black on the outside and the women in white within.
The sole discordant note was that Lu Mingfei, too, was inside the circle... dancing gracefully.

“Hey, is this an empress selection ball? An empress selection ball for the emperor of Austria-Hungary? I’ve seen Sissi. Exactly the same.” Lu Mingfei regretted not kicking Fingel in the face the instant he grabbed him and turning to flee. By the time they were surrounded, it was too late.
Around him, lace-trimmed white gowns bloomed like enormous white flowers as the girls turned.
“Cassell is a German-style college, so Austria-Hungary isn’t far wrong. We have first-rate court-dance instructors.” Fingel was thoroughly absorbed in the dance.
“This is your idea of fighting our way out? Please, we’ve already suffered every humiliation available!”

“Use your head. This is a classical European ball. They’ll change partners!” Fingel strode forward valiantly, speaking under his breath. “Each couple is like XY chromosomes, while we’re two YY chromosomes... Genetically speaking, victory is guaranteed. You know about YY chromosomes? Think back to high-school biology.” His tone was grave and deeply academic. “A man’s chromosomes are XY, a woman’s are XX. Only the so-called ‘supermale’ has the invincible YY! That means however we switch partners, the worst we can end up with is still YY. We can’t lose!”

“I can’t imagine how you fit all those biology handouts and all that optimism into your head. Even now you’re firmly convinced our position is unbeatable.” Lu Mingfei turned with his arms around Fingel’s bearish, tigerish waist, wondering whether to copy the beautiful girls around him and attempt that magnificent high kick. Everyone else was so well synchronized. They were all kicking; he felt his failure to join in might spoil the harmony.

“No,” Fingel said mournfully. “I mean there’s no further defeat available to us. Like a stock that’s hit rock bottom, we can only bounce back. Also, I think you can abandon the idea of doing a split kick. They’re wearing long skirts; you’re wearing pants. Your crotch seam will tear...”
Lu Mingfei did not answer. He suddenly felt as if little crows were flying over his head, cawing away.
“Now! Target the girl with the butterfly hairpin!” As the music changed, Fingel issued his combat order.

The two men advanced with martial valor, clasped arms thrust together like a mortar ready to fire, straight at a pretty girl some ten meters away. She was turning in the arms of a tall, slender young man, her white skirt blossoming, her calves beneath it delicately shaped.
“Senior, you’ve got a great eye!” Lu Mingfei praised him lavishly.

The young man’s expression changed first, then the girl’s. Her white heels nearly tangled; her partner had to steady her before she could stand straight. It was a natural reaction. Anyone would panic at the sight of a mortar composed of two men bearing down on them with murder in its heart.
“Hey, little sis! Don’t fall before I’ve got you in my arms!” Fingel whispered.
The regimented steps of the court dance forced the couple to approach Fingel and Lu Mingfei. Nearer, ever nearer. Five meters, four, three, two...
The girl stepped into a beautiful turn. Her hand slipped free of the boy’s. There was their chance, lasting just an instant!

The two-man mortar split apart. With perfect unanimity, they both leaned out for the girl’s hand like hungry weasels lunging for a chicken. The boy, who had resolved to grit his teeth and finish the group dance, extended a hand that was entirely ignored. His evening coat flared as he spun past the two weasels.
“Me first!” Fingel shoved Lu Mingfei’s shoulder.
“Can’t you give your junior a break?” Lu Mingfei gritted his teeth and held his ground.
That shove opened a narrow gap. The girl’s whirling skirt flashed through it, and just as Fingel was about to kick Lu Mingfei, her hand settled back into her partner’s.
A perfect switch of positions. Butterfly Hairpin sailed away in relief. The two-man mortar looked at each other, heaved a heavy sigh, and reluctantly reassembled.

A stifled laugh sounded nearby. Lu Mingfei looked up dejectedly. Nono had placed her hand in the white-gloved hand of a Japanese boy and was spinning, light as a purple swallowtail butterfly. There it was, that little-witch smile: watching from the sidelines when you were at your worst, laughing in a way you could never decide was adorable or infuriating, grinding a heel into your embarrassed face for good measure. For an instant Lu Mingfei felt angry, and a little hurt.
The very same clothes. Just like that day in the cinema’s VIP auditorium, when the door opened, light streamed in, and this girl stepped through like an angel.
But now she was laughing, laughing at how stupid you looked.
“Damn it, you had to fight me for her. Now neither of us gets her. YY is still YY!” Fingel was furious.
“Screw you! Would we be this embarrassed if you hadn’t lost your head?” Lu Mingfei looked away.
“We’ll have bread, and we’ll have girls! Our own side has to stay united first! This time it’s settled: you get priority!” Fingel sighed.

But there was no next time. The first couple’s quick thinking inspired everyone else. At each change of partners, fluttering white skirts skimmed past just out of reach. The two-man mortar fought on every front and suffered defeat after defeat. Nono was no longer the only one laughing. Elegant laughter rose here and there, spreading among the guests like a plague. Lu Mingfei suspected that if damnable aristocratic etiquette hadn’t required these students to finish the dance, several girls would already have collapsed, pounding the floor with laughter.
“What do we do?” Lu Mingfei hoped Fingel could still come up with something.
“Do about what?” Fingel looked like a man approaching deliverance. “Listen. The music’s ending... Congratulations. You’re the first male partner ever to finish an entire dance with me.”
The music gradually subsided. The men and women bowed to each other with elegant courtly ceremony.
“Retreat!” Fingel ordered.

At that moment the orchestra suddenly rallied. Without a pause it launched into a new introduction, the music positively combative. The partners exchanged startled looks. If the music hadn’t stopped, the dancing wasn’t over. With practiced coordination, they took each other’s hands again.
Another tango.
“Right now I want to murder the conductor’s entire family...” Fingel hugged Lu Mingfei firmly and sighed up at the heavens.

A strange, distorted violin note tore through the dance like a blade. Everyone frowned and looked upstairs. At Cassell College, where the highest quality was required of everything, even an orchestra led by a cook was first-rate. A mistake like that should never have happened.
After drawing out that long note, the first violinist stood, laid her violin on her chair, and headed downstairs.

She was a pale-blond girl in a silver gown set with crystals, her skin almost transparently white, her build petite, poised between child and young woman. Watching her back, Lu Mingfei thought she looked familiar.

The dance continued, but everyone was listening to the footsteps descending from above. The music continued too. The well-trained second violinist took over the lead. However urgently the conductor mouthed at her, the first violinist did not turn back.
Clack!

A pair of silver high heels was set on the marble floor. Their rhinestones refracted dazzling light, like the glass slippers in a fairy tale. The first violinist—or rather, the ice-sculpture girl Lu Mingfei had seen in the 3E exam—took off her black leather shoes and stepped into the heels. They suddenly gave her petite figure height and poise. Her drawn-in stomach and lifted chest lent her a graceful silhouette. Now she was a stunning young woman, though her eternally expressionless face remained frozen in ice.
She slowly raised her arms high and lifted one leg, holding still. It was a classic ballet pose, like a swan dying. So beautiful it made the heart tremble.

She began to dance: a textbook tango, strong and forceful. Spinning, she sliced into the circle along a perfectly straight line, aimed directly at its center, where Lu Mingfei and Fingel stood. Everyone involuntarily made way. The circle split, and the girl cut through like a flash of silver blade. No one could resist her approach. Her dancing was too perfect; she overwhelmed them all with a queen’s commanding presence.
“I get the feeling... she’s not asking me,” Fingel said regretfully. “You are the hot new sensation, after all.”

He did something Lu Mingfei had never expected: pushed him toward the Russian girl, while he himself... spun out through the crowd in the opposite direction, dancing with the same strength and power as she did. Lu Mingfei had to admit Fingel could dance. Perhaps he really had been “Elvis” back in the day.

The instant the Russian girl’s hand touched Lu Mingfei, the music strode valiantly into its climax. With a powerful snap of his head, guided by her strong arms, Lu Mingfei settled into the proper dance position.
Laughter and exclamations died away. Only now did truly splendid dancing begin.

Never in his life had Lu Mingfei imagined he could tango so smoothly. All his dance training amounted to three months of rehearsals for a group number in a Spring Festival show. The visiting instructor had shaken her head repeatedly, saying Lu Mingfei plainly belonged to the category of people whose hands and feet could not work together. If his arms were right, his legs went wrong, and vice versa. In other words, he could either step to the beat with both arms hanging down, or stand still while moving his arms gracefully.
Neither prospect was particularly attractive.
The only reason Lu Mingfei had stuck it out was that Chen Wenwen was his partner.

Yet under the girl’s control and the cues in her eyes, he instantly caught the rhythm. Every movement seemed carved into his mind: where to put his arms, where to step. He did not have to think at all, only relax and follow Her Majesty the Queen of Dance. Their movements were free and flowing, as if they had practiced together for years. Her silver skirt flew, scattering a dazzling confusion of light and shadow.
“Hi... What’s your name?” Lu Mingfei asked hesitantly.
“Zero.” The girl had a slight Russian accent.
“Shouldn’t it be... something-ova or something-na? Zero’s English, isn’t it? As in zero?”
“It’s a Russian word too. It means zero. I have no formal name. The number they gave me was ‘0,’” the girl said evenly. “You can call me Zero.”
“Zero?” Lu Mingfei groped for conversation. “This music sounds familiar.”
“Por Una Cabeza. Its Chinese title is Just One Step Away. By Carlos Gardel, the king of Argentine tango. Have you seen Scent of a Woman?”
Lu Mingfei shook his head.
“Schindler’s List?”

“Yeah, yeah! Won an Oscar, didn’t it? It’d be a bit embarrassing to admit you hadn’t seen that one.” He regretted the words immediately. When a girl like a little Russian queen spun into the dance floor to invite him to dance, he ought to have adopted the air of a Chinese emperor to match her. How had he managed to sound like a hick within two sentences?
“This piece is used in its score. It’s noble music. It looks down on everything.” Zero looked straight into his eyes, her voice perfectly level.

“What do you mean?” Lu Mingfei hardly dared meet her gaze. He did not know why Zero had chosen to save him this way. He had imagined such a scene, but its heroine was supposed to be Nono, now dancing with Caesar.
Maybe she just thought he looked too pathetic and came to his rescue, Lu Mingfei thought.
“I don’t mean anything,” Zero said.

“I know what you mean. I’m not stupid. I think Caesar deliberately gave us the cold shoulder to embarrass us, right? He invited us here, left us hanging, showed us he didn’t care about us at all. Whether I go cling to Chu Zihang’s thigh or Kiran’s calf, he couldn’t care less. He watches us scramble for food, watches us dance like idiots.” Lu Mingfei sighed. “Come to think of it, Caesar’s a great hero with a beautiful girlfriend. Why should he pay attention to a loser? I just had a few days of dumb luck... and started thinking I wasn’t a loser...”
“You don’t have to explain this to me. I told you I don’t mean anything.” Zero interrupted him.
“Really?” Lu Mingfei grew embarrassed again. “I thought...”
“I simply like dancing. I brought my dancing shoes.”
“But why pick me?”
“Everyone else has a partner.”

“Then why not Fingel? He dances better than I do.” Lu Mingfei thought her excuse was painfully flimsy. She liked dancing, so she had sliced through the crowd like a silver knife to take his hand? Was Zero one of those legendary heroines who saved people from fire and flood yet never took the credit?
“Fingel is too tall. Our heights don’t match,” Zero said with conviction.
There was nothing to say. They could only keep dancing.
“At the end, I will turn thirty-six hundred degrees. Hold my hand!” Zero commanded like a queen.

Lu Mingfei obeyed without thinking. In the lingering notes of the finale, the other girls stopped. Zero did not. Pressing her fingers into Lu Mingfei’s palm, she began to spin, skirt flying, silver light whirling from her shoes, her heels beating a quick succession of taps on the floor. For that instant, all the light seemed concentrated on her. To describe her as Tchaikovsky’s dying swan, or as the goddess of Mount Wu in her final song, scattering clouds over the world from Gaotang, would not have been the slightest exaggeration.

The novice dancer Lu Mingfei suddenly felt he had become useful. In high heels, Zero’s petite figure matched his height perfectly, and his raised arm offered her convenient support. Zero drew strength from his hand, using him as the pivot for her turns. If Lu Mingfei suddenly trembled, lost focus, or failed her for any other reason, she would become a top spinning out of balance. He knew perfectly well how unreliable he was, the reigning king of dropping the ball. But Zero had placed her trust in him. This little queen from Russia had staked her superb technique and the nobility that stunned the whole room. What she was gambling for seemed to be...
Lu Mingfei’s dignity.
A beauty’s favor was a weighty debt he had no way to repay. All he could do was focus every scrap of attention on holding Zero’s hand.
Applause. Strong applause. Caesar was actually clapping. Everyone followed his lead. The applause became a storm, and amid that storm the silver swan’s pride reached its zenith.

Lu Mingfei suddenly felt dazed. He had a vague sense that somewhere, sometime, the lights had glittered like this before, the applause had thundered like this before. A slender figure had spun before him under everyone’s gaze, her billowing skirt spreading like a peacock’s tail.
What was going on? When in the past eighteen years had he ever been this spectacular? Impossible, right? It had to be an illusion. How could such imperial magnificence ever belong to him?

But then came confidence, confidence stronger than anything he had ever known, accompanied by a surge of power. He reached out sharply and closed his hand around Zero’s tiny palm. It was the final instant of the dance. Having completed her thirty-six-hundred-degree turn, Zero slowly sank into a curtsy facing him. Her flared skirt folded against her legs, like a flower in full bloom closing into a bud. The timing was flawless, as though Lu Mingfei had signaled her to stop. He himself felt he had merely given an inexplicable twitch and caught the girl’s hand.
Zero had not risen. This was the standard ending for a court dance. Now Lu Mingfei was supposed to return her salute.

Suddenly, he froze. Returning to reality from his splendid imperial feeling, he realized he had never learned court dancing, and naturally had no idea how to bow. The other boys had bowed to their partners at the end of the music, but unfortunately he had paid no attention. His eyes had been fixed on Zero.

Damn it. Was he supposed to kiss her hand? Or just bend at the waist? Put his left hand over his heart, maybe? That would make him look like an Arab. Cold sweat sprang out on his forehead. Such a wonderful dance—surely he wasn’t going to ruin it with the very last detail?
“My beloved minister, you may rise...” In his panic, Lu Mingfei uttered a line so dreadful even he fell apart on hearing it.
“What kind of person am I?” he asked himself, looking around. Only then did he realize no one had heard. They were all applauding hard; the clapping had drowned out his terrible line.

Zero rose. Without looking at Lu Mingfei, she walked to the edge of the floor, changed back into her black leather shoes, slipped the silver heels into their bags and then into a black case, accepted a long crimson coat from a waiter, and draped it over herself. Without saying goodbye to anyone, she went straight out the front door. She had arrived as sharp as a blade; her departure could not have been more understated.
“This year’s freshmen are really interesting,” Lu Mingfei heard Caesar say quietly.
Holding a brandy on the rocks, Caesar watched Zero’s back as it was about to disappear into the darkness.
“And now, our Student Council president, Caesar, will address us.” A department head tapped the microphone on the second-floor landing.

The discussion of Zero subsided. Dazzling as the Russian freshman was, Caesar was, after all, the college’s undisputed star. He handed his glass to a waiter, ascended the curving stairs, and stood at the microphone, surveying everyone below like an emperor inspecting his army.
“On my first day at this college, I was deeply disappointed.” Caesar paused. “Because there were too many people here!”
“The true elite will never be the majority!”

What an opening. Cold enough to give you goose bumps. Lu Mingfei thought that if this man ruled the world, he would probably join Hitler and become a fascist. And the first people he would eliminate would be losers like Lu Mingfei.
But then Caesar smiled faintly. “Thank you all for coming. I’m delighted to see the finest of the elite gathered here. Guests of the Gattuso family”—he raised one finger—“can only be the elite!”

For a moment there was silence, then someone began clapping vigorously. Everyone joined in, eyes shining with excitement. It was a rare honor to be regarded by Caesar as the finest of their generation.

Lu Mingfei felt a little flattered too. Apparently he counted among the outstanding... But he did not quite understand why the person leading the applause was none other than Fingel, whose expression fell just short of tears. This F-rank loser of a senior seemed profoundly moved by Caesar’s appreciation, forgetting he had only come along with Lu Mingfei and wasn’t on the guest list at all.

“I like working with outstanding people. My time is limited, and I cannot tolerate wasting it on those who fall short.” Caesar gestured for silence. “I have always believed Cassell College is a miracle, entrusted with an immense mission. It should therefore be the finest among us who speak with the greatest clarity and force.”
“Who should speak with that voice?” He gazed coldly down at them.
“Caesar!” one of his Student Council followers suddenly shouted.
“No. Not me, but... us!” Caesar raised his voice. “The finest among us. We!”

The redoubled applause nearly burst Lu Mingfei’s eardrums. He had grown up in a socialist country, where high-school politics class taught that the voice of the people was the loudest of all. But wedged among these self-proclaimed elites, and counted as one himself, he could only clap along.

“Since the day I took over, the Student Council has not served everyone. Why are we here? To kill Dragon Kings? Preserve the world? Or prove ourselves?” Caesar shrugged. “Tell other people what you do, and they’ll think you’re mad.”

“But the true elite will always seem mad to the mundane world! Nietzsche, for instance! He is dead, but he was the true elite of his age.” Like a fired-up ancient Greek orator, Caesar swept his arms forcefully. “Because ordinary people cannot tolerate anyone unlike themselves! Nor can they tolerate the elite, because they are stupid!”
In the students’ shining eyes, Lu Mingfei saw the declaration: “I’m a madman rejected by the mundane world!”

Caesar spread his hands. “I have no wish to drive anyone from this campus. Since the rules of Cassell College allow those who fall short to study here, I can accept that. I understand perfectly well that such people have their own ways of surviving, and I have no desire to interfere. But I hope they will refrain from making too much noise. I dislike noise.”

“But in the end, this college and this mission must be sustained by the finest!” He pointed skyward again. “Now, allow me, as your current Student Council president, to welcome you to the ranks of the mad!”

Looking up at him, Lu Mingfei thought of the Buddha Shakyamuni, who on the day of his birth had walked seven steps in each of the four directions, pointed at heaven and earth, and declared, “In heaven and on earth, I alone am supreme.”
“Could you possibly be a little less full of yourself?” he thought. “Don’t you know people stomp on anyone who gets too cocky?”
In fact, he could have said it aloud. No one was paying him any attention. Everyone was clapping, then embracing each other in excitement.
“Should we hug too? Otherwise we’ll look really out of place.” Fingel wriggled into view behind him.
“I don’t want to hug a man... And I can’t bear to watch a loser like you join the Student Council.” Lu Mingfei glanced at him. “You don’t mind getting trampled to death by the elite?”
“No... I hear Caesar’s a pretty good boss. Pays allowances to Student Council members out of his own pocket.”
“Could you have just a little self-respect...” Lu Mingfei covered his face again. There had been far too many face-covering occasions lately.
“Lu Mingfei!” Caesar’s voice came from above.
Startled, Lu Mingfei looked up. Caesar was holding out a hand toward him from the landing. “Come up and stand beside me.” Then he gave a cold smile. “You may refuse.”

Lu Mingfei’s mind went blank. Everyone was watching. The moment of choice had arrived. If he went up and stood beside Caesar, tomorrow the campus news site would announce his accession to the Student Council, and Chu Zihang would instantly become his enemy. If he refused... In short, going up meant opposing Chu Zihang, and staying down meant opposing Caesar. Caesar had no intention of giving him time to think. This wasn’t even like joining the Communist Youth League: no application to write, no vetting required.

He really wouldn’t mind following Caesar. In fact, when Fingel mentioned that this rich young master paid allowances to his followers from his own pocket, Lu Mingfei’s heart had stirred a little too...
He simply wasn’t ready to offend Chu Zihang yet.
Dead silence.
Then Caesar’s phone rang. Taken aback, he reached into his pocket.

All through the hall, cell phones erupted in a cacophony: musical ringtones, buzzers, the ding-a-ling of old-fashioned telephones, alerts for unknown callers. Scores upon scores of different tones sounded at the same instant, as if a marching band had suddenly struck up all around them. Few people had ever heard so many phones ring at once. It set their hearts pounding.

After a moment’s shock, every guest began searching for a phone. The girls had hidden theirs in all sorts of places: tucked into stockings, concealed in the folds of full skirts, entrusted to their dance partners. The sight of a hundred people fumbling frantically for phones made Lu Mingfei let out a long breath. He had no phone anyway and couldn’t be bothered about who was calling. At least this spared him a decision. He looked around, preparing to slip away.
Caesar opened his phone. After a single sentence, his expression changed abruptly. He raised a hand for silence, held up the phone, and switched on the speaker.
“...Please go to the windows and look toward the college gates. Hold your breath. When guests come calling, the host should be ready.” The voice on the phone was low and electronically altered.
Everyone else’s expression changed too. The same voice was coming from every phone.
The guests surged toward the windows. Through Amber Hall’s enormous floor-to-ceiling panes, they could see the closed ornamental cast-iron gates, lit by a cold lamp.

A tremendous boom deafened them for an instant. In the blinding firelight, the iron gates twisted and were hurled into the air by the blast, rising twenty meters before falling back to smash into the ground. Alarms rang across campus. In the night, every building suddenly lit up. The quiet darkness was utterly shattered.
Red alert went into effect at once.

Brilliant beams of light poured into the campus with the roar of motorcycles. Clad in black combat uniforms, the intruders sped in on snarling Black Widow motorcycles, guns gleaming cruelly in their hands. Once inside they scattered, firing with precision to shatter every security camera they passed.
“What? What?” Lu Mingfei cried. “A challenge match? Colleges raid each other’s turf too?”
The intruders really did look far too much like a biker gang.
“This is the beginning... of our war!” The caller gave a chilling laugh and hung up.

“Red alert! Red alert! Dragon incursion! Dragon incursion! Freshmen are to remain in their dormitories. Students who have passed Battlefield Survival are to collect weapons immediately. Load Frigga rounds. Live ammunition is prohibited.” Norma’s voice carried through loudspeakers to every corner of campus. “Seal all entrances. You are authorized to fire on unidentified persons.”
“Dragon incursion?” Lu Mingfei stared. “Dragons... invading on motorcycles? This isn’t another Freedom Day, is it? Isn’t there only one a year?”

The grave expressions around him showed this was no drill. Students who had just been gliding about in evening wear instantly assumed the bearing of trained soldiers, streaming outside in orderly ranks. Maintenance staff parked vehicles outside every building and opened the compartments, revealing neatly racked automatic weapons. In front of Amber Hall came a dense clatter of guns being cocked.

Beneath a starless sky, a dark figure stood on a corner tower of Cassell College, watching the motorcycle lights scatter like fireflies into every corner of the campus and go out. People poured from the buildings and secured every passage and entrance. This peaceful campus had abruptly become a heavily guarded military fortress.

He tossed his phone from the tower, pulled on a mask, and produced another. “Everything’s going according to your plan. The operation has begun. But isn’t this entrance a little too much like putting on a show?”
“Whether this operation succeeds or not, I want to leave a lasting impression,” the person on the other end said with a laugh.
“Then you couldn’t have picked a better man. I always leave”—the man on the tower spoke coldly—“a lasting impression!”

Suddenly he leaped over the railing, arms spread, plunging through the air. The tower was eight meters high, a drop whose impact would have snapped an ordinary person’s spine. He landed with an easy roll, sprinted forward in a leopard’s crouch, and vanished into the darkness.

In the library control room, Manstein and Guderian hurried through the door. Professor von Schneider stood before the large screen, studying the points of light that filled it. Each point represented a student taking part in the alert.
“A dragon incursion? What’s going on? Who classified this as a dragon incursion?” Manstein looked tense.

He had thought a “dragon incursion” was something that existed only in theory. For over a century, every dragon on the verge of waking had been killed before it could leave its tomb. Since when did these creatures get to swagger into headquarters? And dragons in a group? That stretched the imagination too far.

“Norma. I lack sufficient clearance to learn why she classified it as a dragon incursion, but the intruders have indisputably arrived.” Schneider brought up footage of the instant the motorcycles entered campus.
He turned. At the sight of Guderian, he froze, then grew angry. “What are you wearing?”
Guderian looked down at himself. “Combat fatigues... Though I know I won’t be much use in a fight.”

He had gone to bed early and been startled out of a dream, but he hadn’t forgotten emergency procedure. He had pulled on the combat uniform he hadn’t worn for years and, with considerable effort, loaded Frigga rounds into the magazine. He had almost forgotten how to cock a pistol.
“But you’re wearing a nightcap!”
“Oh. So I am.” Sheepishly Guderian removed the red nightcap. He now looked somewhat less like Santa Claus.
“Could it be a false alarm from Norma?” Manstein asked. “There are about ten of them. An incursion on this scale—what for? Sabotage? A show of force?”
“My guess is they’re after something,” Schneider said quietly.

“Something?” Manstein frowned. “If you mean money, this college has any number of antiques that would fetch high prices at auction. If you mean value, everything in the Ice Cellar could be called priceless. What do you mean?”
“Compared with this, the rest are nothing. I mean...” Schneider met Manstein’s eyes. “What the principal brought back from China!”
“The principal’s back?” Guderian blinked. “I wasn’t informed.”

“He informed no one. But half an hour ago, a helicopter landed in the hangar. An hour ago, an extra run of the CC1000 train arrived at the station. Only the principal can add a train without going through me,” Schneider said. “Of course, there’s an even simpler piece of evidence. You need only log in to a freshman’s inbox.”
Using A-rank authorization, Schneider logged in to the student mail group. There was a mass email:
Dear students,

I am delighted to have returned from China alive. The good news is that we have made a tremendous gain in China. There is bad news too. All students taking my classes should note that attendance will be taken in all three courses I teach next week.
Good luck.
Your faithful friend,
Anjou
P.S. I am considering giving a quiz before classes begin and counting it toward your grades.
“This email was sent to the freshmen enrolled in his courses half an hour ago,” Schneider said.
“What he brought back from China is... the bone vessel of the Dragon King Norton,” Manstein said. “That explains it. The bone vessel arrived half an hour ago, and the incursion followed immediately.”
“Where is it now?” Guderian asked.
“It must be in the most heavily guarded place: the Ice Cellar. So our defense must focus on the underground levels,” Schneider said.

Manstein nodded. “Three main entrances: Valhalla, the chapel, and the library. Norma defends the library, but Valhalla and the chapel are vulnerable. How many people can the Executive Department deploy?”

“Very few. The campus has never been invaded since the college was founded, so our Executive Department agents are all overseas on search assignments. We must rely on the students. Trained students with exceptional bloodlines are our main force. Caesar Gattuso is leading the Student Council in defense of Valhalla, and Chu Zihang is leading the Lionheart Society at the chapel,” Schneider said. “Their bloodlines mean their actual abilities already exceed those of the vast majority of Executive Department agents.”
“There’s no other choice.” Manstein said, “Can we reach the principal?”

“I called his cell. It’s switched off. Sometimes he really is difficult. He brings something of this caliber back to campus without telling anyone, leaving us no time to establish security, then sends an email about his class schedule.” Schneider shook his head.
“So he really is an educator!” Guderian said.
“Hey, hey, hey! Can someone escort me back to my dorm?” Lu Mingfei looked left and right. “Any of you guys with guns willing to walk me back? It’s a long way, and those people have guns!”

No one paid attention. Students hurried past Amber Hall, each team with a leader assigning defenses within its sector. Sniper rifles were set up on high ground. Groups of several people swiftly took advantageous positions, spreading out in squads while flashlight beams crisscrossed the darkness.
Outside Amber Hall, Lu Mingfei was almost hopping with frustration.
“Walk back yourself.” Someone spoke behind him. “No one’s going to eat you. Keep acting like this and everyone will look down on our S-rank.”
He turned. Nono stood in the light behind him, arms folded, leaning against a pillar.
“This is a matter of life and death, okay? Dragon incursion! Who cares about dignity now?” Lu Mingfei said. “You think this is some midnight training march?”
“Then what should we do? Everyone else is busy. Want your big sis to walk you back?” Nono asked.
“That works...”
“But I haven’t even picked up a weapon.” Nono shrugged. “If we actually run into them, two shots and we’re both done.”
Lu Mingfei looked around. “Right, Fingel! He’s in his eighth year, built like a tank. He must have some skills, right?”
“Huh? Our loser senior’s gone.” He slapped his forehead. “Of course. Given his loyalty rating, he probably wouldn’t remember to call me when he slipped away.”
“Since no one’s taking you back, why don’t we go out and have some fun?” Nono patted his shoulder.
“What? Isn’t the whole college on alert for a dragon incursion? Though I haven’t seen so much as a dragon hair...”
“We’ll be safe outside. Aren’t the intruders wandering around inside the campus right now?”
“Good point. But if we get caught, will they come down hard on us?” Lu Mingfei was tempted. “Expulsion?”
“Nothing that serious. At worst they’ll dock our fieldwork grades. Come or don’t. I’m going.” Nono turned and walked away.
Lu Mingfei blinked, then ran after her. “Hey, hey! Where are we going?”

“Bugatti Veyron. Made at the German Volkswagen company’s factory in the French town of Molsheim. Sixteen cylinders, four turbochargers...” Nono pulled off the rain cover, exposing a silver-gray sports car under the lights. The car started by remote control, its lights flashing, its engine’s heavy rumble like a dragon’s roar.

“One thousand and one horsepower, top speed four hundred and seven kilometers an hour, zero to a hundred in just two-point-five seconds... This thing...” Lu Mingfei sighed in admiration. “I’ve seen it in magazines!”
“Now it’s yours. Caesar lost it to you. He put it up as his stake for this year’s Freedom Day, betting against Chu Zihang’s Murasame. And you won.”
“Isn’t that a bit extravagant? This car costs a million euros!” Lu Mingfei caught the keys Nono tossed him.
“He doesn’t care. Caesar doesn’t actually like this car. It was a birthday present from his father. He considers a playboy-style sports car like this an insult.”
“Does his dad need a godson?” The words “Please adopt me” were written in Lu Mingfei’s eyes.
“You drive. I’m tired.”

The Bugatti’s retractable hardtop opened. Nono took off her high heels, hopped in, and settled into the passenger seat. Lu Mingfei hopped in too, gripped the steering wheel, drew a deep breath, and stared silently at the sky.
“Savoring the thrill of winning a supercar?” Nono asked.
“No. Deciding whether I should hit the gas first or change gears...” Following his instincts, Lu Mingfei stepped on the accelerator.

Amid screams, the tires smoked against the road and the Bugatti bolted like a wild horse freed of its reins. Nono laughed and laughed, pulled out the silver pin holding up her hair, bit it between her teeth, and let her long hair down. Suddenly Lu Mingfei remembered Fingel saying Nono was actually a little crazy.
You could never understand what she was thinking.

The dark figure switched off his Black Widow and drew a black shotgun with a sawed-off barrel from the rear motorcycle bag. It was a very intimidating weapon. He stroked the grip, rather pleased with himself. With the power of life and death in his hands, he felt immensely glorious.
His position was excellent, in a blind corner no one passed.

He took out his phone and dialed a number. A recorded message answered: “Number 13. Your target is Valhalla. Use the supplied identity card to pass the access controls. Once inside, locate the entrance to the central computer room, then listen for further instructions.”

His number in the team was thirteen, the last. It sounded unlucky, but it made him feel as dashing as the Grim Reaper. This wasn’t his first assignment; he had always been a man who cared about the right feeling. Each member of the team would follow different instructions, then rendezvous, to avoid an ambush wiping them all out.
“Valhalla.” Number 13 repeated the name silently.
“Crap!” He froze. He had brought all his equipment, but no map. The campus was full of buildings that looked much the same. Which was Valhalla?
He had no sense of direction. In his own estimation, it was his only flaw.
“No choice. A real man can always shoot his way out, right?” Number 13 tightened his grip on the gun and encouraged himself.
“But a real expert doesn’t resort to violence lightly,” he thought again. “If you can send a Ghost to drop a nuke, don’t send in battlecruisers for a frontal bombardment.”
The Bugatti passed through the blasted gates, turned onto the road, and met the mountain wind head-on.

Since he had been carried in unconscious, this was Lu Mingfei’s first view of the campus from outside. Only now did he discover it stood halfway up a mountain, a road winding past its gates. In the distance, layers of conifer forest in the valleys rose and fell in the wind like black waves.
“It’s called the mountaintop campus, but it isn’t actually at the summit. It’s halfway up. At the foot are the station and the valley campus,” Nono said. “We’re going to the summit.”
“What’s at the summit?”
“Stars.”

There were no other cars on the mountain road. The headlights lit one bend warning sign after another. As they wound higher, Lu Mingfei gradually got the hang of controlling the car. He glanced at Nono. Her long lashes were lowered, her head tilted to one side, her face quiet. For a moment the world was peaceful and beautiful. Even the engine seemed to rumble more softly.
The lights swept over a sign ahead: BEWARE OF BEARS.
“Bears?” Lu Mingfei blinked.
“Yes. Lots of bears on this mountain.” A clear boy’s voice beside him.
Lu Mingfei jumped. He turned to see Lu Mingze sitting in the passenger seat, hands on his knees like an obedient middle-schooler.
“Aah! When did you jump in? Can you stop turning up out of nowhere without making a sound? It’s like a haunting, you know?” Lu Mingfei broke into a cold sweat.
“Watch the road. Drive carefully. There’s a turn ahead,” Lu Mingze said evenly.

“Whenever I see you, it’s a dream anyway. Why bother driving carefully? Even if I hit a tree, I’ll just wake up, right? Please, what sort of restless ghost are you, always pestering me?” Lu Mingfei was furious. Any other time, fine, but when he was driving a famous car along a mountain road with the girl he liked, couldn’t this guy have the sense to make himself scarce?
“It isn’t entirely a dream. There really is a turn ahead. If you don’t steer, we’re all going to die,” the boy said.

As the yellow traffic sign flashed before his eyes, cold sweat burst out all over Lu Mingfei and he wrenched the wheel. Fortunately, the Bugatti’s chassis was superb, and it took the ninety-degree bend smoothly. Two seconds later and they would have flown off the cliff. Lu Mingze did not so much as blink.
“Damn it, we nearly died! Please stop scaring me like that! It’s your fault I couldn’t see the road!” Lu Mingfei complained.
“I only came to remind you there was a bend. Without me, a novice driver like you would probably have died with the woman he likes.” Lu Mingze’s face remained a blank.
“What woman I like? She’s just a classmate.” Lu Mingfei felt a little guilty. “What did you call her? A woman? You sound like some old man!”
“You may fool other people about these things, but you can’t fool me.” Lu Mingze shrugged. “Need a little help?”
“You’d be helping if you stopped appearing out of nowhere like a ghost.”
“Remember what Nono said you needed to court a girl? Music, flowers, and a beautiful declaration.” Lu Mingze ignored his grumbling entirely.
Lu Mingfei stared. “You even know about that?”
“For music, you can use this car’s sound system. Do you need me to write the declaration?”
“Pah!”

“Since I can’t help with those, I’ll help you send flowers! New cheat unlocked: ‘show me the flowers.’ Say it aloud, like a magic spell. Try it. It’s fun. But you can’t use it until an hour from now, and it’s only good tonight,” Lu Mingze said. “I won’t wish you luck, because things won’t end well for you and her.”
“Then why come here playing the good guy?”
“Nothing wrong with pitying you!” Lu Mingze smiled coldly.
Lu Mingfei thought the brat’s doom-mongering tongue was insufferable beyond belief. Without thinking, he reached over and thumped him on the head. Lu Mingze made no sound of protest.

Lu Mingfei realized something was wrong. Looking again, he saw his fist had struck the headrest of Nono’s seat. Her soft, warm cheek was less than a centimeter from his hand. She was still sleeping, her breath falling on his fist.
“Oh! This is the part of the script where you stroke the heroine’s cheek, she suddenly opens her eyes, your gazes lock, and sparks fly!”
“Goddamn it, that Lu Mingze... What a...” A battle raged in Lu Mingfei’s heart.
After a long time, he slowly withdrew his hand. “What an obnoxious little brat.”
“What brat?” Nono woke and heard his muttering.

“Nothing. You misheard. I said ‘little tortoise.’ A little tortoise just crawled past beside me. I hate things like that, creeping up without a sound so you don’t even notice.” Lu Mingfei stared straight ahead, hands gripping the wheel.
Number 13 was delighted with himself. He felt like a bat flying through the night, lightly crossing rooftop after rooftop.
His brothers in Brooklyn, New York, called him “Cheetah,” but he thought that lacked the glamour of a bat, that bewitching hint of the vampire.

The campus defenses were much tighter than he had imagined, but they couldn’t stop Number 13. He wasn’t advancing at ground level at all. He had brought a grappling gun, purchased at great expense from a buddy who developed weapons for the military. It could fire a rope-tethered spike into rock from dozens of meters away. Number 13 followed these ropes right over the students’ heads, immensely pleased with himself.
He had always had confidence in himself.
There was only one problem: he could no longer find the rendezvous point. Perched on rooftops beyond everyone’s sight, he had lost his way around the campus.
“Now I understand the importance of scouting!” he muttered to himself.
The winding mountain road ended at a stone tablet blocking the way. Lu Mingfei stopped before it.
“Switch on the high beams,” Nono said.

Brilliant shafts of light stabbed like swords into the distant sky, illuminating the whole summit. The ground was flat, with few trees, and covered in grass. A spring bubbled from beneath some rocks into a little mountaintop lake. Overflowing water spilled down the mountain as a snowy-white waterfall, its faint sound drifting up from below.
“No stars.” Nono stretched out, leaned against the seat back, and looked at the sky.
No kidding, Lu Mingfei thought. It had just rained, and the sky was pitch-black. He had realized as soon as they left the gates that there was nothing to see up here.
So why had he still eagerly volunteered as chauffeur?
“What a big guy,” Nono said.
“What big guy? Is there a bear?” Lu Mingfei craned his neck.

“I mean it’s quiet,” Nono said. “Didn’t you tell Professor Manstein that ‘big guy’ was Chinese slang for quiet? So now in class he keeps telling his students, ‘Please be big guy. Stay big guy. A little more big guy...’ He thinks he’s being witty, showing off his knowledge of slang.”
Lu Mingfei silently covered his face. Sooner or later someone would tell Professor Manstein that this was pure nonsense. He was taking Manstein’s course too. Would he fail?
“Want to soak our feet in the spring?” Nono asked.

With that she hopped over the door in just her stockings. Lu Mingfei followed her, stumbling across the autumn meadow toward the splashing sound of the mountaintop spring lake. The only light came from the Bugatti behind them. Reflected in the spring, it seemed to coat the water with silver. Nono chose a rock and sat down, then noticed Lu Mingfei studying her curiously.
“What are you looking at?”
“I was wondering...” Lu Mingfei told the truth. “Whether you need me to turn around before you can take off your stockings.”
Nono made a face at him, produced a delicate pair of scissors from her bag, and cut the stockings around her ankles, baring her feet.
“It’s cold. You’ll need guts!” Nono said.
“As a man who once swam the Yangtze in winter, how could soaking my feet in a little cold water trouble me?” Lu Mingfei chose a rock too, sat down, and pulled off his socks.

They exchanged a look and slowly lowered their feet into the spring together. The cold burrowed into every pore, then shot up their spines. Both shuddered at the same moment. As they did it, each stared intently at the other’s face, hoping to catch an amusing change of expression. They held out with all their might, but finally the same corner of each mouth twitched.
“You’re faking it!” They pointed at each other and burst into wild, unrestrained laughter.
“It’ll warm up after a while, then get cold again. We have to leave before it gets cold the second time,” Nono said. “You really swim in winter?”
“Like hell. I hate the cold.” Hugging himself, Lu Mingfei chanted, “The freezing wind will be my death; tomorrow I’ll build a nest.”
Just as Nono had said, once the initial chill passed, their feet gradually grew warm. With all his blood concentrated on heating his feet, Lu Mingfei felt rather comfortable.

“So what exactly did Caesar mean by all that?” He chatted idly with Nono. “Inviting us to the ball, then giving us the cold shoulder. Such a big production, all those other guests, all-you-can-eat lobster. Just to watch us make fools of ourselves? Those roses at the entrance scared me. Fingel even said they were for me.”
“Roses?” Nono looked up at him, then burst out laughing.

“Those roses weren’t for you. They were for me,” she said. “The reception wasn’t thrown especially for you either. It was a celebration for me. Actually, I was the one who invited you. Caesar just said he wanted to speak with you face-to-face too.”

“So Xiang Yu wasn’t giving the feast. His beauty Yu Ji was hosting!” Lu Mingfei nodded like a chicken pecking grain. A beauty’s favor was a weighty gift, and he was delighted. “I thought it was a Hongmen banquet, a trap. I even brought Fingel along as my Fan Kuai!”
“My motives for inviting you weren’t pure either. What are you so happy about?” Nono rolled her eyes at him.
“I’m not!” Lu Mingfei blushed a little. Fortunately, it was very dark.
“Why are you blushing?” Nono asked.
“A glow of vigor!” Lu Mingfei declared loudly, striking the pose of Yang Zirong marching up the mountain to fight the tiger.
“I’m teasing. It’s so dark I can’t see,” Nono said.
Only then did Lu Mingfei realize he had given himself away. The headlights were behind him, and Nono hadn’t even glanced at him out of the corner of her eye.

“I invited you because I’m not used to being around Caesar’s followers,” Nono said. “I know he put a lot of thought into it, but it feels strange. Everyone was invited just to see how splendid the two of us are. I have to accept his good intentions and keep smiling while his followers wish me happiness and take it for granted I’m Caesar’s fiancée. There wasn’t a single fun person at the whole party.”
“Fiancée?” Lu Mingfei froze for a moment. An engagement sounded terribly weighty, heavy enough to slow his heartbeat.
“Today’s my birthday.” After a silence, Nono said it casually. But her voice was as light as a breath of wind, easily missed if you weren’t listening.
“Happy birthday!” Lu Mingfei blurted.
Then he froze. Unprepared. Completely unprepared.

Once he had stood in line all morning to buy Chen Wenwen an autographed CD, then eagerly delivered it. His reward had been a polite “Thank you,” which satisfied him perfectly. He didn’t care that her desk also held a Swarovski crystal pendant from someone else and other gift boxes of unknown contents. To him, a morning in line for such an important day was nothing. He had never expected his present to be the best. A passing grade would do. He set low standards for himself.

He had never thought to ask Nono’s birthday. Even if he had, why would he buy her a present? They didn’t know each other well. There was no reason. And then his gift wouldn’t be competing with a Swarovski crystal pendant, but Tahitian pearls or limited-edition Van Cleef & Arpels jewelry, delivered by a blond Caesar in a supercar.
Now, for no reason at all, Nono had told him directly, while he sat barefoot, without even his socks.
Beyond that dry little greeting, perhaps all he could do was pull the white handkerchief from his jacket pocket, fold it into a boat, and float it over.
He hurriedly felt in his pocket... and discovered that the handkerchief had already been used to wipe his mouth while he and Fingel devoured lobster.
“Received,” Nono said lightly.
“Caesar put on all that for you?” Lu Mingfei had to concede defeat. “Talk about grandeur. No wonder it looked like an empress selection ball.”
“But I don’t like it, and I can hardly refuse his kindness,” Nono said. “He’s stubborn. Once he puts thought into something, he wants you to tell him he’s wonderful.”
Her tone was casual, as though she were discussing a complete stranger who had nothing to do with her.
Something stirred in Lu Mingfei’s heart. Suddenly he asked, “Do you like Caesar?”
“Of course. If I didn’t, why would I be with him? Do you think I’m stupid?” Nono curled her lip.

Lu Mingfei scratched his head, turning the words over in his stomach several times before letting them out. “But sometimes it seems... you barely pay him any attention... And he doesn’t seem to interfere with you much either.”
Nono considered. “Lots of girls at the college pursue Caesar. Guess why he chose me.”
Lu Mingfei looked her up and down, utterly confident. “Small waist, long legs, pretty face!”
“The girl who asked you to dance today had a small waist, long legs, and a very pretty face too. Did you take the chance to ask for her number?”
“I’m not Caesar! My type is...” Lu Mingfei’s tongue tangled. Apparently his type was rather like Caesar’s after all.

“Caesar thinks he was born to lead. Everything has to be the best: the strongest abilities, the finest team, the most outstanding girlfriend. Only his grades don’t have to be the best; he thinks those are meaningless. He likes me because I’m one of the college’s very few girls with A-rank blood. He thinks I’m the only A-rank who’s a match for him, so he chose me.”
Lu Mingfei was a little startled. “Bloodline ranks are good for that too? Then I’m S-rank. If I were a girl, Caesar would definitely dump you and pick me?”
“With your talent and looks, I suppose I’d be heartbroken if you were a girl.” Nono looked him up and down too, paying particular attention to his chest, waist, and legs.
“Hey! What a sleazy look...” Lu Mingfei wrapped his jacket more tightly around himself against the cold wind.

“But a Caesar like that suits me best. A boy thinks I’m wonderful, so he likes me. I happen to think I really am wonderful and deserve to be liked. I think he’s pretty good too, and he doesn’t make me uncomfortable. Isn’t that rather nice?” Nono said lightly.
“As long as he doesn’t make you uncomfortable... that’s enough?” Lu Mingfei couldn’t understand.

“Mm. I don’t ask much, though you could say I ask a great deal. Lots of people make me uncomfortable. But being with you is quite comfortable too, junior... Every time I see you, I want to grab you and bully you a little.” Nono stuck out her tongue. “If I had a boyfriend like you, I’d laugh and bully him from morning till night.”
“Hey! Hey! There you go again...”

“Do you think I’m unreasonable?” Nono raised her lovely eyebrows. “Caesar practically says, ‘Only you are worthy of me. Boys as splendid as us deserve the finest girls as accessories.’ Yet I don’t mind being an accessory at all.”
“None of my business.” Lu Mingfei looked away.
“I don’t mind, because it’s simple. If I’m not good enough, I don’t have to use anything to force Caesar to stay with me. The reverse is true too. We’re well matched.”
“Well matched?” Lu Mingfei found the words rather grating, like “families of equal standing.”
But family standing really was important, wasn’t it? In ancient China, the person writing a story about a rich young lady falling for a poor scholar was bound to be another poor scholar.

“Since I don’t quite understand how to love someone, I find someone who matches me.” Nono kicked the icy water; crystalline splashes danced on her toes. “I used to read romances, and I could never understand those heroines crying their eyes out, asking, ‘Do you love me or not? Have your feelings changed?’ It can all be so simple. If someone likes you, he’ll naturally come hold you and tell you. If he doesn’t like you anymore, crying at him won’t help. Right?”

“Then why did you teach me how to pursue Chen Wenwen? By your logic, there’s no need to pursue girls. If she likes me, she’ll tell me, and if she doesn’t, chasing her is useless.” Lu Mingfei thought Nono was peddling twisted logic.
“Chen Wenwen’s different,” Nono said. “I think this way because I’m strange.”
“What’s strange about you?”

“Caesar knows. People who don’t know me well don’t.” Nono stretched. “The best thing about Caesar is his confidence. Even when he knows you’re strange, the big guy’s brimming with heroic spirit, absolutely certain he can handle you. ‘Who but I could seal away a demoness like her?’ ‘For world peace, stand back and let me battle this witch!’”
“Pfft.” Lu Mingfei thrust out his chest. “If the witch has a small waist and long legs, we’re all heroes. Who’d hang back?”
Nono blinked, looking him up and down. “You’re not talking about yourself, are you? Come on then, brother, if you’ve got the guts. Don’t cry when you get blown to pieces.”
“A gentleman’s word!” Lu Mingfei suddenly roared. Some damned nerve had twitched. The words had bypassed his brain and leaped naturally from his mouth, thunderous and commanding.
Nono was taken aback, but could only complete the saying: “Can’t be overtaken by a team of four horses!”
The dark figures pressed against the wall, concealed in the gap between Valhalla and Rhine Hall, listening to hurried footsteps pass outside.

Valhalla and Rhine Hall were twin buildings, separated by a gap less than twenty centimeters wide, ordinarily too narrow for an adult. Yet a full twelve people were squeezed inside. These rigorously trained people had drawn in their rib cages, making their bodies thin enough to fit. That was why they remained undiscovered. Flashlight beams swept past constantly, but none had been aimed into this blind spot.

“Captain, security’s tight. If we’d known and sneaked in instead of worrying about making an entrance... wouldn’t this have been a lot easier?” One dark figure whispered to the slender silhouette ahead.
“Shut up! It’s tactics!” the captain hissed.

In front of subordinates, the captain could hardly admit to having a few regrets too. Who could have guessed this seemingly peaceful college would have such a rigorous defensive system once an emergency began?
“We’ve lost Number 13,” someone behind added.
“That’s tactics too!” The captain was getting impatient.
“Mai, I’ve never seen you in such a sorry state.” An icy voice came from the back of the line.

At some unknown moment a thirteenth person had appeared behind them all, but it wasn’t Number 13. He was small and thin, with no markings on his black combat uniform, his face masked. Through the voice-changing device, his voice sounded exceedingly caustic. The man ahead of him silently broke into a cold sweat. This newcomer had appeared like a flickering ghost. If he hadn’t been on their side, a single gentle thrust of a knife would already have killed him.
“Number 13!” someone whispered sharply.
The captain looked up toward the library roof nearby and asked softly, “Who said that guy from Brooklyn was a professional?”
“His résumé... He really did perform well on previous assignments,” someone whispered.
The captain turned and slapped that person across the face. There was another person between them, and no one could see how the slap had traveled across.
“A professional one-man show, you mean?” The captain was close to losing it.

On the library roof, a gecko-like fellow had assumed a thoroughly professional pose, body low, binoculars trained on the activity below. It was their missing Number 13. The original plan had them enter separately and rendezvous at Valhalla. But the tight security had left them huddled in this crack like cockroaches, while Number 13 was now flying noiselessly and stylishly between rooftops, displaying his batlike form to the full.
“If you don’t know the way, it doesn’t matter how cool you look running!” the captain cursed under their breath.
“Don’t shift the blame. The person in charge must own their mistakes,” the last person in line said coldly.
“I don’t need reminding. I’m the captain of this operation. Naturally, I have a way to fix it.”

The captain took out a phone. Having to make a call at a moment like this felt rather stupid. Shaking their head, the captain said, “Hey. Stop eating chips and think of something. We’re trapped. Security here isn’t nearly as lax as you claimed.”
“Mm. Then we’ll have to activate the backup plan,” the person on the phone said.
“What backup plan?”
“The plan for when Mai’s infiltration gets blocked.”
“You knew in advance we’d be blocked?” Obvious anger entered the captain’s voice.

“It’s easy to understand. We still don’t know what sort of man Anjou is. He’s been principal of Cassell College for decades. Do you think he’s an idiot who’d make a careless mistake and give you an opening?” The voice on the phone was relaxed. “That’s why we arranged for Number 13.”
“That king of the one-man show? Please! I think he’s lost right now!” The captain was flabbergasted.

“Deliberately. The equipment I gave him included no map. From what I know, he’s the sort of hopeless navigator who’d get lost driving two blocks from his own home to buy a burger. So he was bound not to find Valhalla.”
“What kind of backup plan is this?” the captain raged.
“A lab mouse that doesn’t know the way will head for the most obvious target. That’s his preset objective. As for you, all you need to do is wait.”

“For what? I’m a cockroach wedged in a crack. There are hundreds of people outside. The moment I show myself, I’ll be spotted. I can’t use Yanling. The Night Watcher controls the surrounding domain. His Yanling: Edict is too powerful. I’m completely suppressed!”

The caller chuckled softly. “The Night Watcher will end Edict soon. Since they can’t find you, their sense of danger will make them try to use Yanling. That’s your chance. Once you can use yours, who could find you?”
Professor Schneider checked his watch. A full hour had passed, and the intruders still hadn’t been found.
Once the emergency was triggered, every camera had gone into operation. Each entrance and exit was under strict surveillance. They could not have escaped the campus either.
The extraordinary calm unsettled him. What should have happened hadn’t. That was dangerous. He could not fathom the enemy’s identity or intention, and the feeling haunted him like a ghost.
“Is there anyone here besides Ye Sheng who can use Yanling: Snake?” He turned to Manstein.
“I’m not authorized to view the confidential Yanling files. But there’s at least one other. Myself.”
“Your Yanling is Snake?”

“My domain is three times larger than Ye Sheng’s. If I could use Yanling, perhaps I could locate the intruders. But under the Night Watcher’s Edict”—Manstein pointed to his temple—“our power is forced into sleep.”
“Could we ask the Night Watcher to end Edict?” Schneider asked tentatively.
“My father?” Manstein blinked. “Impossible. Only the principal can order him to end Edict.”

“This is an unusual situation. We cannot obtain the principal’s authorization. But once Edict is ended, we’ll have seven hundred Yanling-capable students as a fighting force. Our strength will be unprecedented. Just for tonight. Could you try?” Schneider stared into Manstein’s eyes.
After a long silence, Manstein picked up the phone. “I can only try. That old cowboy... He’s the sort who makes no exceptions, even for family.”
In the attic of the chapel bell tower, the classic 1952 Western High Noon was playing. Marshal Gary Cooper walked the dusty street of a frontier town with a gun at his hip.

The viewer was dressed much like Gary Cooper: plaid shirt, curled-brim hat, cowboy boots with shining spurs. The old fellow reclined on the sofa like an enormous potato, feet propped high, a beer bottle dangling from his hand. When the phone rang, he picked up the receiver.
“Still watching High Noon? Aren’t you tired of it after so many times?”
“Hey! Anjou! You’re back at the college?” The old cowboy’s eyes lit up.
“Yes, and I found the bones of the Dragon King Norton. I’m about to run an MRI reconstruction,” the principal said. “I suggest switching to Scent of a Woman.”
“I know you don’t like hot-blooded films,” the old cowboy said. “You’re a randy old devil.”
“Mm. Listen. End Edict.”
The old cowboy suddenly sat straight, set down his beer, and slowly grew serious. “Are you serious?”

“There are intruders. Norma classifies it as a dragon incursion. Wouldn’t it be good to give the youngsters some practice?” the principal said evenly. “The dragon princes will soon awaken. They need experience.”
“Yanling is a devil in a bottle. Letting it out lightly may grant you power, but that isn’t necessarily a good thing. Are the youngsters ready?”
“Those who carry dragon blood are already using the devil’s power to fight the devil, aren’t they? This world will soon be beyond the two of us to protect. We need young people.”
After a long silence, the old cowboy said, “I’ll agree for now. Keep your students under control.”
He switched off the television and sat quietly on the sofa. Only a candle on the table lit his aged face. How many years had that candle been burning? Twelve, or fifteen? He could no longer remember.
The phone rang again.
“Who is it?” The old cowboy picked up.
“Dad.” The person on the other end sounded rather nervous.
“Hey! Manstein, my son! Good evening! Is your cold better? I’ve missed you terribly!” The old cowboy suddenly beamed.
“Dad, I caught that cold three weeks ago. A cold gets better on its own in two weeks even without medicine.” Manstein sighed.
“Oh... Really?” The old cowboy scratched his head. “Is there something you need, son?”

“I wanted to... ask whether you could... I know it may violate college rules, but tonight is an exceptional situation. There are intruders, and we can’t find them. There are some very important things in the college that may be their targets.” After a long hesitation, Manstein said, “Could you... temporarily end Edict? This is a joint request from Professor Schneider of the Executive Department and myself.”
The old cowboy stared silently at the ceiling, saying nothing for a long time.
“I know this call oversteps my authority. Sorry to interrupt your film.” After enduring the silence, Manstein was eager to hang up.
“Oh... No, no!” the old cowboy said. “I was thinking. Your birthday’s in two weeks, isn’t it, my dear son?”
“Yes.” Manstein was a little embarrassed. “I’m surprised you remember.”

“Then... consider it my birthday present! I’ll end Edict immediately, as a birthday gift to you. I’m a good father who’ll break college rules for his beloved son!” the old cowboy vowed. “Son, you’ll learn what a blessing it is to have a father!”
Utterly bewildered, Manstein hung up.
“Well?” Schneider looked at him. “If he won’t agree, never mind.”

“No... He agreed...” Manstein rubbed his bald scalp. “But it feels... so strange. When I was young, he was the sort of father who never took me on roller coasters for my birthday. You could never find him, day or night. He drank and gambled. And now he says... he’s giving me this as a birthday present.”
“Enjoy this belated fatherly love!” Guderian patted his old friend’s shoulder.
“That isn’t the point, all right?” Manstein glared.

Up in the attic, the old cowboy drained his beer, sat up straight on the sofa, and blew out the candle on the table. As its flame died, a spirit powerful enough to envelop all of Cassell College dispersed. Dozens of meters below the library, dozens, even hundreds, of silver-blue shafts of light slowly rose on the central processing system’s monitoring screen: powers handed down from primeval times.
The students stirred. Their long-suppressed spirits had awakened.
Almost at the same instant, the captain leaped out of the gap. Amid chanted Draconic, the figure grew blacker and blacker, until it was black as a mass of ink.
Yanling: Dark Illumination.
On landing, the figure dissolved, as if it had always been an ink stain, washed from paper by a splash of water.
“Stay close to me. My domain extends roughly two meters around me.” The captain’s voice reached every companion’s ears.
At that very moment a student passed less than a meter away, entirely unaware of the wisp of dark smoke brushing his body beneath the streetlamp.
Beside the mountaintop spring lake, Nono leaned half her body out to look down the mountain. At that angle, one careless move would send her tumbling.
“Hey!” Lu Mingfei couldn’t quite bring himself to grab her. “Fall and you’re dead.”
“Not a single firefly left,” Nono muttered.
“Firefly?”

“The stars I meant are a kind of big firefly. In summer they fly up along the waterfall from below. It’s beautiful. There’s lots of mist in summer too, so they look like stars rising through a cloud,” Nono said. “Think I’m stupid? That I wouldn’t notice it was cloudy until I reached the summit?”

Lu Mingfei swore inwardly. This senior really was a witch, wasn’t she? She could read everything he thought, even the things buried deep... Though come to think of it, he didn’t have any very deep thoughts.
Lu Mingfei was eighteen, with a life as lovely and blank as a white sheet of paper, and about one hair’s breadth of depth.

“Have you heard of Guixu, the Returning Abyss?” Nono stared at the waterfall. “They say there’s a place in the sea where the seabed disappears. When seawater reaches it, it becomes an enormous waterfall, dropping thousands upon thousands of li. If you fall in, you never reach the bottom. You starve to death on the way down...” Her voice was very soft. “Souls slowly rise like fireflies, following the stars, drifting home.”
Lu Mingfei stared helplessly. This ocean-deep fable exceeded the thinking capacity of his blank sheet of paper.
“Hey. Were you serious?” Nono was still looking down. “I can say yes. You have that privilege of courting any girl for three months without being refused, right? I can give you three months.”
Lu Mingfei trembled. He had thought the unthinking words he had blurted earlier had been automatically erased by their silence.
“Heh... I guess on day one Caesar would use that knife of his, Dictator or whatever, to turn me into Dongfang Bubai, the castrated Invincible of the East?” He scratched his head.
“So you were planning to climb into my bed too? I thought you just meant dinner dates and movies.” His witch of a senior turned to him with curious eyes.
Lu Mingfei’s mouth fell open. No sound emerged. This chatterbox had lost the power of speech. You could have stuffed an egg in his mouth.
“All right. I’m joking.” Nono shrugged. “Every time I see you, I want to bully you a little. Don’t you think you’re funny?”
Nono went on pinning up her hair. Lu Mingfei hung his head, feeling utterly and completely defeated.
“Now I’m going to be a lobbyist,” Nono said. “How about it? Join the Student Council.”
“Is this Caesar’s honey trap?” Lu Mingfei blinked, disappointed. Here, where fireflies drifted up from below in summer, this was what Nono wanted to discuss.
“Not really. It has nothing to do with Caesar.”
“Nothing to do with him?” Only a ghost would believe that, Lu Mingfei thought.

“You don’t understand Caesar yet. He’s a politician, but he’s conceited. He won’t spend time winning people over. He thinks he’s a leader worthy of trust, so you ought to follow him. If you won’t, he can’t be bothered with you. At most, when you become an obstacle, he’ll blast you away... This invitation is mine. It has nothing to do with Caesar’s position. Your joining would benefit me.”
“Benefit you?”
Nono tilted her head. “Then I’d have my very first follower.”
“What do you need followers for? Aren’t Caesar’s followers yours?”
“He’s him, and I’m me. I’m Caesar’s girlfriend, not the lady of the Student Council.” Something occurred to Nono. “Oh. Sorry.”
“Sorry?” Lu Mingfei didn’t understand.
“Someone in the Student Council signaled the orchestra to keep playing. Probably wanted to prolong your humiliation,” Nono said. “But it wasn’t Caesar. He doesn’t pay that much attention to you yet.”
“It’s fine,” Lu Mingfei said. “It was really Fingel’s fault for going crazy, spouting nonsense about ‘I used to be an Elvis too’ and making it impossible to back out.”
“I actually wanted to rescue you, but Caesar would have been unhappy.” Nono shrugged. “Had to protect the host’s dignity.”

Something stirred in Lu Mingfei’s heart. He lowered his head to look at his feet in the spring. So Nono had thought about rescuing him again. Yet she had laughed so happily then, he hadn’t sensed a thing. It really was hard to understand what this girl was thinking.
He had felt some resentment toward Nono then, hadn’t he? Why? Because she had saved him once, so he took it for granted that she would step out and give him a hand again?
Completely unreasonable.

“Don’t make it sound like all I do is wait for you to save me. If I had the chance, I’d help you with something too...
