Though I don’t suppose there’s anything left for me to do.” Lu Mingfei tried to sound casual. “You’re so capable. You think everything through, and you can handle everything yourself.”
“You can help me right now.”
“Huh?”

“Give me a birthday present. I imagine Caesar has something ready, but right now he’s probably scouring the campus for those intruders, competing with Chu Zihang to see who finds them first.” Nono spoke lightly. “A girl needs presents on her birthday. They make her feel she matters.”
“I... I didn’t prepare anything...” Sweat instantly sprang out on Lu Mingfei’s forehead.
“Then let’s see you improvise, junior.” Nono spread her hands. “You can’t go through the world with everything prepared.”
Lu Mingfei scratched his head. “Actually, I have a handkerchief. I could have folded you a little boat and floated it over.”
“Junior, I never knew you had such romantic ideas! Confess! What romance novel did you get that from?” Nono’s eyes narrowed with laughter.

“But...” Lu Mingfei pulled the crumpled handkerchief from his pants pocket and unfolded it for her. It was a riot of colors, from mustard green to mayonnaise yellow to chili-sauce red, like a faded floral bedsheet.
Nono wrinkled her brow. “Gross! You two use such a jumble of sauces for sashimi!”
Sheepishly, Lu Mingfei stuffed the handkerchief back into his pocket. “Won’t Caesar come running over with your present tomorrow morning?”
“Birthday presents can’t be early or late. They have to reach someone while she’s waiting, and you have to say ‘Happy birthday’ to her yourself,” Nono said. “If you’re late, it’s different.”
Lu Mingfei froze. Suddenly he remembered Professor Guderian telling him, “Mingfei, Mom and Dad love you.”

It was true. Some things had to be said in person, at exactly the right time and place. He had seen people gossiping about Ye Sheng and Aki on the campus discussion board, saying they must have liked each other very much. He remembered Nono joking at the dinner table, “Why aren’t you two married yet?” Now the moment had passed. Saying it again would be useless.

In the beautiful comic artist Xia Da’s book Zi Bu Yu, Things the Master Would Not Speak Of, a line went, “To miss something isn’t to be mistaken. It’s to have let it pass.” That was probably what it meant.
Nono took out her phone and set it on a rock beside her. It was an Apple iPhone, its rounded back reflecting the light.
“I was born at nine fifteen at night. Let’s see if anyone calls to give me a present before nine fifteen,” Nono said.
Nine fifteen. Lu Mingfei blinked. That time sounded familiar.
“Oh, come on. Even if Caesar doesn’t make it, surely you’ve got plenty of other people giving you gifts?” Lu Mingfei thought of the dozens Chen Wenwen received on one birthday.
“No. Caesar’s aura of kingly domination scared all the potential suitors away.” Nono smiled. “Speaking of which, anywhere you want to visit now you’re in America?”

“New York,” Lu Mingfei said. “I only know one friend in America. He’s called Old Tang. We used to play StarCraft together. He said if I came to America, he’d take me around on Greyhounds.” (Author’s note: Greyhound is a long-distance bus service. In America, most families have cars, and Greyhound is regarded as transportation for poor people.)
“Greyhound? That’s fun,” Nono said.
“When you have Bugatti Veyrons and Ferraris to drive and still say Greyhound’s good, it makes you sound awfully charitable toward kids from poor families.”

“No. Greyhound has its own good points. You follow it along and get off wherever you think looks nice. No driving, no planning directions. It’s like rolling dice to see where your travels take you,” Nono said. “Tell me about your past. Pass the time.”
“Then if I tell you mine, you have to tell me yours. That’s fair.”
“Mm.” Nono thought. “On your birthday, it’ll be my turn.”
“All right! It’s a deal!”
Lu Mingfei couldn’t remember how long he talked that night. From Chen Wenwen to Liu Miaomiao, from Chu Zihang to Zhao Menghua, from warm feet to cold feet, until finally he was shivering a little.
Toward the end he suddenly realized he was the only one talking, and he didn’t know whether Nono was listening. Her eyes sometimes rested on her phone, sometimes on the infinite distance.
“All right. Let’s go.” Nono checked her watch and put away her phone.
“Sure. Okay.” Lu Mingfei stood too, dusting off his backside. “Were you waiting for someone to call?”
Nono blinked, then smiled with narrowed eyes. “Yes. I was waiting for someone to give me a present.”
“Not Caesar?”
“Not Caesar.”
“Then who?”
“Not telling.”
“Now you’re being all tsundere.”
“What’s tsundere about a girl waiting for a birthday present?” Nono sprang up. “I really was waiting for someone to give me one.”
Shoes in hand, Nono walked ahead, softly humming a song. Lu Mingfei followed close behind. Brilliant headlights shone before them.
“Have you ever received a birthday present?” Nono asked casually.

“Yes.” Lu Mingfei thought about it. His uncle did give him a little something on his birthday. Occasionally classmates gave him gifts too. To repay him for the CD, for instance, Chen Wenwen had given him a pen.
“I never have,” Nono said.
“No way.” Lu Mingfei didn’t believe her.

“I was stubborn as a kid. I wouldn’t tell anyone my birthday. I thought it was my own secret.” Hands behind her back, Nono stood at the cliff’s edge and looked at the sky. “Only later did I realize secrets aren’t any fun if you never tell anyone. If you keep your birthday secret, no one gives you presents. But deep down, you still want them... You’re just too awkward to say so.”
“What about Caesar?”
“He only just found out. He checked my enrollment records. I never actually told him either.”
Lu Mingfei felt a little dazed. At that moment, in his eyes, this commanding girl named Chen Motong suddenly became terribly, terribly lonely. A lonely, slender girl.
He checked his watch. It was just past nine fifteen. Like a flash of lightning, he remembered something.
“Show me... the flowers...” he whispered, as though reciting an ancient spell.
Number 13 crawled out of a fireplace, coated in so much charcoal ash he looked as though he had come from Africa.

From the rooftop he had studied the terrain. Almost every building was under heavy surveillance except the one he stood on, which was also quite a distinctive landmark. For some reason, it was a blind spot in the defensive network. So he decided to enter. Perhaps from inside he could find a route to the underground garage.
“A library?” Number 13 muttered.

Neat cherrywood shelves were filled with scholarly books bearing gilt titles. Green lamps shone on broad cherrywood desks, but no one was there. The books had alarming names: Studies in Dragon Genetics, Dragon Skeletons: The Superevolution of Reptiles, Ritual Procedures of Dragon Worship...

Number 13 was a Dungeons & Dragons player who spent weekends in a café serving as GM for tabletop games. He had even played a red dragon. But he couldn’t believe there were actually people in the world who studied dragons as real creatures, and did so with such scholarly rigor.
A campus full of lunatics.
“Oh yeah!” he cheered.
Beside a bookshelf stood the thing of his dreams: a campus map. The entire college’s layout was clearly shown, down to the underground passages.

An underground passage led straight from the library where he stood to an area marked in red: “ICE CELLAR: ALCHEMICAL EQUIPMENT AND SPECIMEN EXHIBITION HALL.” More red lettering followed: “EXTREME DANGER! NO ENTRY WITHOUT SPECIAL AUTHORIZATION!”
“Isn’t this... a little too easy?” Number 13 felt the joy of having a windfall drop into his lap.

He was a bounty hunter who earned money taking jobs from a secret website. This assignment had been rated 3A, extremely difficult, with an exceptionally high reward. Countless people had wanted it, but only he had passed the employer’s screening. Those rejected had all said the danger must be extraordinary. In this business, reward was always proportional to risk. But now this “Ice Cellar” didn’t seem like an easily defended stronghold at all. It was just an exhibition hall, with no fewer than three underground passages leading to it.

He had to praise Lady Luck. Drawing a cup of cola from the dispenser beside him, he forgot all about meeting up at Valhalla and headed for the entrance to the underground passage while studying the map.
The map showed that the passage reached the Ice Cellar by way of the Central Mainframe Control Room. Beside it was a person’s name: “Norma.”

Guderian glanced at Manstein, seated on the sofa with his eyes tightly shut, directing his Snakes in a search of the entire campus. The Snakes’ strength lay in finding metal. Finding people took longer.
Guderian stood beside Schneider and stared with him at the campus map on the screen. Points of light were densely stationed in every sector. Only one building was almost blank.
“You haven’t posted defenses in the library? The Central Mainframe Control Room and the Ice Cellar are our two most important locations, and there’s no one there.” Guderian pointed to the blank area.

“I’m only worried about the entrances in Valhalla and the chapel. Through the library entrance, no one can penetrate the Central Mainframe Control Room. Norma is there. Her self-defense system is the most powerful on campus. The moment she detects danger, she can electrify the whole metal passage with hundreds of thousands of volts. Not even a mosquito could survive!” Schneider said.
A cell phone vibrated.
Number 13 answered. “Hello?”

“Your second instruction: once you reach the library, use the black card provided to enter the underground level. Pass through the Central Mainframe Control Room and proceed to the Ice Cellar. More detailed instructions will follow.” The recording ended. That damned woman on the recording always left things half-said. Number 13 spat.

CENTRAL MAINFRAME CONTROL ROOM read the sign over the entrance before him. After cutting the security camera’s power cable, he approached the heavy metal door, knocked on it, and found himself at a loss.
He couldn’t begin to guess how thick it was. Knocking on it was like knocking on a steel ingot.

He took the black card from his pants pocket. It had been mailed to him with the rest of his equipment before the operation: a black card without a single marking. He swiped it through the access reader. After a beep, slow mechanical sounds came from inside the metal door. Twelve wrist-thick locking bolts slowly withdrew, and the twenty-centimeter-thick door swung open with a boom.
Access granted.

Number 13 stared in astonishment at the black card, then at the dark corridor before him. Metal plates covered every surface. Red lights stretched to the far end. Infrared beams formed a thicket, the gaps between them scarcely two fingers wide. Even a rat couldn’t squeeze through. Cameras looked down from both sides every few meters, so densely placed there was no blind spot.
Yet now all these rigorous surveillance systems were shutting down for him. The infrared beams winked out one by one. The cameras powered off. Red lights turned green in succession.
Within seconds the corridor was completely open, green lights all the way.
“Whew!” Number 13 walked down the corridor, patting the drooping cameras, inwardly ecstatic at his dumb luck.
What kind of security system was this? One black card defeated the whole thing. All for show.

What he didn’t know was that another lethal system had shut down for him too: the deadly high-voltage static field between the metal plates, reaching hundreds of thousands of volts. Normally, even a mosquito entering this space would have been instantly charred. He reached the end and entered an enormous chamber, evidently the mainframe room. Black metal boxes were stacked from floor to ceiling, countless blade processors assembled together. Indicator lights flickered at high speed. This colossal system, several stories tall, was processing vast quantities of data.
“Now that’s high-tech!” Number 13 marveled.
“Hee-ha, hee-ha, hee-ha, hee-ha, hee-ha!”
The odd sound startled Number 13. He drew his gun and spun around.
“Good evening! Would you care for a drink, sir? Wonderful evening, isn’t it?”

At the end of his shotgun barrel stood a metal puppet half a person’s height, made of a heap of glittering short metal rods, like a child’s magnetic toy. But the thing was not merely bowing; its comical face even wore a fawning smile.
“Don’t come any closer... Come closer and I... I’ll blow you apart!” Unsure what he was facing, Number 13 couldn’t help feeling nervous.
“My name is Adams. We offer beer and pretty girls!” The little thing could not have been more obliging.
“Wh-what... What kind of advanced toy is this?” Number 13 couldn’t take it anymore. He lashed out with a flying kick and scattered the puppet into a heap of little metal rods.
The rods rolled around and actually assembled themselves back into the puppet, which trundled off behind Number 13. “EVA, someone’s trashing our place! EVA, someone’s trashing our place!”
“What the hell is going on?” Number 13 turned. His heart gave a violent spasm and almost stopped for an instant.
“Hey. Good evening!” He smiled and spoke involuntarily.

Behind him, a faint shaft of light shone down from above. An almost transparent figure stood within it: a long-haired girl in silk pajamas, so lovely she seemed unreal. Number 13 felt both excited and ashamed of his own ugliness. Dazedly, he felt he had blundered into someone’s bedroom.
The girl actually nodded to him. “Who are you?”
Number 13 hesitated. “Just a passerby.”
He realized she was only a hologram, but her lifelike manner still made him want to speak to her as a person.

“You have entered the Central Mainframe Control Room without authorization. The college has no record of you. I was built in 2001. You used a privileged-access card preset before my construction. I should raise the alarm, but I cannot. I know you are an enemy, but your authorization requires me to treat you as an ally,” the girl said. “So this is my final warning: leave immediately. That is best for you.”
“Leave immediately? Come on... I...” Number 13 scratched his head. “I rode a motorcycle all the way here... I’m exhausted.”
The girl watched him in silence.
“Since I have a privileged-access card... then... Sorry, could I ask directions... Which way is the Ice Cellar?” Number 13 asked very carefully.
The girl pointed.
“Oh. Okay. Thanks.” Number 13 had no idea what expression to wear.
At the corner, he turned and told the girl, “Goodbye.”
She watched him silently from behind. Number 13 gazed into her clear eyes and, for some reason, felt a chill inside.
Lu Mingfei looked all around, hoping to see something miraculous happen.

After the last time, he had great faith in Lu Mingze’s so-called cheats. But he was intensely curious: how could flowers be delivered to a mountaintop on a night like this? Would a UPS van suddenly drive up, a courier jump out and say, “Hi, sir! Roses you ordered?” Or would a helicopter sweep across the sky and drop a bouquet?
But there were no headlights on the mountain road, no aircraft in the sky. Every possibility was closed off.

A meteor-like light crossed the sky, but it traveled upward. High overhead, a point of light exploded into a magnificent flower. Hundreds of streams of light fell, illuminating their faces in an instant.
“Fireworks!” Nono stopped short, then jumped up, pointing at the sky.

Fireworks kept shooting up from below, like meteors in reverse. Flower seeds scattered through the sky, blooming wildly in the darkness: dandelions like purple suns, cascading blue-green spider plants, roses woven from red and gold, white dahlias... Lu Mingfei had never seen anyone set off fireworks so extravagantly, turning the night sky into a basket of flowers in a single instant.
The flowers Lu Mingze had promised had arrived. Once again, he had proved he would not disappoint Lu Mingfei.
Lu Mingfei turned his head. In the light of the fireworks, a faint glow flowed over Nono’s profile, along with fine traces of tears.
He did not know why she was crying. A moment ago she had been waving her arms like a child who had never seen fireworks. An instant later, tears were flowing.
“So beautiful,” Nono whispered.

After a brief silence, one last enormous firework shell rose into the sky. At the very zenith, it burst. Violet, lake green, water blue, moon white, gosling yellow... Lights of every color formed words against a vast golden background:
“NoNo, Happy Birthday!”
“Is it...” Nono whispered. “For me?”
“Y-yes!” Lu Mingfei wore an odd expression. “It says NoNo. That means Nono, right... Unless it means ‘No No, happy birthday.’ Who’d have such a weird name?”
Nono smacked his forehead hard. “Whose name is weird? Your name’s weird!”
Lu Mingfei rubbed his forehead and grinned.
“How lovely... Whoever sent it.” Nono watched the slowly fading sky and spoke softly.

Suddenly she smiled, reached out and thoroughly tousled Lu Mingfei’s hair, then turned and walked away. He stood stupidly and let her, watching her steps suddenly grow as light as a little deer’s. After a long daze, he broke into a run after her.
Lu Mingfei skipped along behind Nono, his heart full of happiness. Turning toward the surrounding darkness, he stretched out both hands and gave two thumbs-up.
He wanted to say, Thank you, thank you! You’re amazing! Lu Mingze, wherever you are, you’re one truly amazing little bastard.
From somewhere came the faintest hint of laughter, cold and disdainful. Lu Mingfei looked around. No one was there.
“You sure she said nono? The name is weird!” In the valley, a Green Forest Fireworks truck stood parked while its crew cleaned up the site.
“Who knows? She said it, she paid it, so we made it! Who cares? I guess she is a Chinese, you know some Chinese have a lot of money!” his coworker said.
The two Green Forest Fireworks employees were very pleased with the pay for this last-minute job, though one hour had been a bit of a rush.
